channel.title: CHEN, Yiru - Research Radar
channel.description: Daily ranked academic article recommendations from Research Radar.

item.title: [Research Radar: Relevant #1] Interpretable, flexible and spatially aware integration of multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets from diverse sources
item.description: Source: Nature Genetics | Published: 2026-04-27 | DOI: 10.1038/s41588-026-02579-x | Recommendation: READ FULL | Summary: INSPIRE combines deep learning with non-negative matrix factorization to integrate diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets, recovering shared and context-specific spatial gene programs and tissue organization across scales. | Why it matters: Spatial transcriptomics integration across platforms and cohorts is a central bottleneck. INSPIRE targets this directly with an interpretable factorization approach. | Why for Yiru: Directly addresses method development for cross-cohort spatial transcriptomics — a core interest.

item.title: [Research Radar: Relevant #2] Spatial 5mC-seq profiling of embryos and decidua after implantation in mammals
item.description: Source: Nature Methods | Published: 2026-04-27 | DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03079-w | Recommendation: READ FULL | Summary: Spatial 5mC-seq enables unbiased, spatiotemporal genome-wide methylome profiling at single-cell resolution in mammalian embryos and decidua. | Why it matters: Expands spatial omics beyond transcript measurements into the methylome — opens a new axis for linking cell state with spatial context. | Why for Yiru: A high-impact spatial epigenomics method that broadens the spatial toolkit beyond RNA/protein readouts.

item.title: [Research Radar: Relevant #3] Tumor-derived branched-chain α-keto acids activate Notch signaling in tumor-associated macrophages to limit immunity
item.description: Source: Nature Immunology | Published: 2026-04-14 | DOI: 10.1038/s41590-026-02484-9 | Recommendation: READ FULL | Summary: Tumor cells release branched-chain amino acid metabolites that bind and activate Notch on tumor-associated macrophages, reprogramming them toward an immunosuppressive state. | Why it matters: Reveals a direct metabolic-immune signaling axis through which tumors co-opt macrophages — both a mechanistic insight and a potential therapeutic node. | Why for Yiru: Tumor microenvironment, macrophage biology, and immunotherapy are core interests. This paper connects tumor metabolism to immune evasion through a specific molecular pathway.

item.title: [Research Radar: Relevant #4] Diet-induced metabolic memory shapes CD8+ T cell ferroptosis susceptibility
item.description: Source: Nature Immunology | Published: 2026-04-13 | DOI: 10.1038/s41590-026-02493-8 | Recommendation: READ FULL | Summary: Transient or continuous high-fat diet induces metabolic changes in CD8+ T cells that increase vulnerability to ferroptosis and reduce anti-tumor responses. A xanthine-dependent antioxidant program shields CD8+ T cells from ferroptosis. | Why it matters: Connects diet-induced metabolic memory to T cell fitness in tumors — a clinically actionable axis for improving immunotherapy. | Why for Yiru: CD8 T cell biology and anti-tumor immunity with a metabolism angle — directly relevant to computational immunology interests.

item.title: [Research Radar: Relevant #5] Global genetic interaction network of a human cell maps conserved principles and informs functional interpretation of gene co-essentiality profiles
item.description: Source: Cell | Published: 2026-04-26 | DOI: | Recommendation: READ FULL | Summary: CRISPR perturbation of ~4 million gene pairs in human HAP1 cells maps ~89,000 genetic interactions, revealing a hierarchical network linking genes to complexes, pathways, and cellular processes. Elucidates genes underlying cancer cell genetic dependencies. | Why it matters: A massive-scale genetic interaction map at human cell resolution — a foundational resource for interpreting functional genomics and cancer dependencies. | Why for Yiru: Large-scale CRISPR screening with computational systems-level analysis — methodological and biological interests align.

item.title: [Research Radar: Breakthrough #1] How artificial intelligence is reengineering protein engineering
item.description: Source: Science | Published: 2026-04-09 | DOI: 10.1126/science.aec8444 | Recommendation: SKIM | Summary: A review of how computational modeling and high-throughput wet-lab experiments have matured protein engineering into a broad field with applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, agriculture, and manufacturing. | Why it matters: Shows how AI has transformed a core biological engineering discipline — a mature example of AI-for-science that may foreshadow similar transformations in other bio domains. | Why for Yiru: Not core spatial omics, but the AI-for-biology paradigm is worth tracking as it increasingly intersects with systems biology and biomedical AI.

item.title: [Research Radar: Breakthrough #2] Clinical trials for continuously monitored and updated AI systems
item.description: Source: Nature Medicine | Published: 2026-04-27 | DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04368-9 | Recommendation: SKIM | Summary: As AI becomes embedded in clinical workflows, clinical trials must accommodate ongoing monitoring and updates rather than treating AI as a static intervention. | Why it matters: Addresses a growing gap between AI development velocity and clinical evidence standards — critical for biomedical AI translation. | Why for Yiru: Biomedical AI is a long-term direction; understanding the evolving regulatory and clinical validation landscape is strategically relevant.

item.title: [Research Radar: Breakthrough #3] An inducible base editing platform for cancer functional genomics in vivo
item.description: Source: Nature Biotechnology | Published: 2026-04-15 | DOI: 10.1038/s41587-026-03079-3 | Recommendation: SKIM | Summary: A small-molecule-controllable base editor enables gene editing with reduced toxicity and minimal transcriptional perturbation, enabling in vivo inducible genetic screening and systematic identification of critical residues in cancer therapeutic targets. | Why it matters: In vivo functional genomics has been limited by editing toxicity — this platform opens the door to direct in-tumor genetic screens. | Why for Yiru: Broader than the core spatial omics focus, but in vivo CRISPR technology is becoming an essential complement to spatial readout methods.
